questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: What does the idiom 'to burn the midnight oil' mean?
options: To work or study late into the night
questions.correctAnswer: To work or study late into the night
questions.explanation: 'To burn the midnight oil' means to work or study late at night (when oil lamps would be burning). 'To waste resources' is wrong — that would be 'to pour money down the drain'. 'To start a fire' is wrong — the idiom is figurative, not literal. 'To cook at midnight' is wrong — it refers to working/studying, not cooking.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about idioms:

(i) 'A piece of cake' means something very easy.
(ii) 'Break the ice' means to initiate conversation in an awkward situation.
(iii) 'Spill the beans' means to cook beans badly.
(iv) 'Hit the nail on the head' means to be exactly right.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'a piece of cake' means very easy. (ii) is correct — 'break the ice' means to ease tension and start conversation. (iv) is correct — 'hit the nail on the head' means to describe something precisely or be exactly right. (iii) is wrong — 'spill the beans' means to reveal a secret unintentionally, NOT to cook beans badly.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The idiom 'to let the cat out of the bag' means:
questions.explanation: 'To let the cat out of the bag' means to accidentally reveal something that was meant to be kept secret. 'To release a pet' is wrong — the idiom is figurative, not about actual animals. 'To be cruel to animals' is wrong — it has nothing to do with animal cruelty. 'To pack carelessly' is wrong — it's about disclosing secrets, not packing.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: 'Once in a blue moon'
questions.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' means something that happens very rarely or almost never. 'Every night' is wrong — the idiom emphasizes rarity, not frequency. 'During full moon' is wrong — it's not about actual moon phases. 'When the sky is blue' is wrong — it has nothing to do with sky colour.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Idioms cannot be understood by their literal meanings.
Reason (R): Idioms are figurative expressions whose meanings are established by convention and usage, not by the individual meanings of their component words.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — idioms like 'kick the bucket' (die) cannot be understood literally. Reason (R) is also correct — idioms derive meaning from cultural convention, not from individual word meanings. (R) explains (A) because the figurative/conventional nature of idioms is exactly why literal interpretation fails. Option 2 is wrong because (R) directly explains (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is correct. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following idioms with their meanings:

Column I:
(a) To bell the cat
(b) A wild goose chase
(c) To cry over spilt milk
(d) To turn over a new leaf

Column II:
(i) To make a fresh start in life
(ii) A hopeless and useless pursuit
(iii) To take a risky lead in a dangerous task
(iv) To regret something that cannot be undone

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'To bell the cat' = to take a dangerous initiative that others are afraid of — matches (iii). (b) 'A wild goose chase' = a pointless, hopeless pursuit — matches (ii). (c) 'To cry over spilt milk' = to regret what cannot be changed — matches (iv). (d) 'To turn over a new leaf' = to begin a new, better phase of life — matches (i). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b). Option 3 swaps (b) and (c). Option 4 swaps (c) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The phrase 'to add fuel to the fire' means:
options: To make a bad situation worse
questions.correctAnswer: To make a bad situation worse
questions.explanation: 'To add fuel to the fire' means to worsen an already problematic situation through one's words or actions. 'To start a campfire' is wrong — the idiom is figurative. 'To cook faster' is wrong — it's not about cooking. 'To extinguish a fire' is wrong — adding fuel does the OPPOSITE of extinguishing.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following idioms mean 'to die'?

(i) To kick the bucket
(ii) To bite the dust
(iii) To burn bridges
(iv) To pass away

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'Kick the bucket' = to die (informal/slang) ✓. (ii) 'Bite the dust' = to die or be defeated ✓. (iv) 'Pass away' = to die (euphemism) ✓. (iii) 'Burn bridges' is wrong — it means to destroy relationships or eliminate the possibility of returning, NOT to die.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The idiom 'to have a bee in one's bonnet' means:
options: To be obsessed with a particular idea
To be stung by an insect
To keep bees as a hobby
questions.correctAnswer: To be obsessed with a particular idea
questions.explanation: 'To have a bee in one's bonnet' means to be preoccupied or obsessed with a particular idea that one keeps talking about. 'To be stung' is wrong — the idiom is figurative. 'To wear a fancy hat' is wrong — 'bonnet' here is incidental. 'To keep bees' is wrong — it's not about apiculture.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about idioms:

(i) 'To eat humble pie' means to admit one's mistake and apologize.
(ii) 'To blow one's own trumpet' means to boast about oneself.
(iii) 'To bury the hatchet' means to start a fight.
(iv) 'To beat around the bush' means to avoid coming to the main point.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'eat humble pie' means to humbly apologize after being proved wrong. (ii) is correct — 'blow one's own trumpet' means to praise oneself/boast. (iv) is correct — 'beat around the bush' means to talk around the subject without reaching the point. (iii) is wrong — 'bury the hatchet' means to make PEACE or end a quarrel, NOT to start a fight.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: What does the idiom 'to turn a blind eye' mean?
options: To look the other way while driving
questions.explanation: 'To turn a blind eye' means to knowingly pretend not to notice something wrong. 'Poor eyesight' is wrong — the idiom is about deliberate ignorance, not physical blindness. 'Looking away while driving' is wrong — it's not about driving. 'Blinking rapidly' is wrong — it has nothing to do with blinking.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The idiom 'Rome was not built in a day' means that important things take time to accomplish.
Reason (R): Rome was a great empire that took centuries to build, so the idiom uses this historical reference to teach patience.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — the idiom conveys that great achievements require patience and time. Reason (R) is also correct — the reference to Rome's gradual construction over centuries illustrates the point. (R) explains (A) by providing the historical basis for the idiom's meaning. Option 2 is wrong because (R) directly explains (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is historically reasonable. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The idiom 'to pull someone's leg' means:
options: To joke with or tease someone
questions.correctAnswer: To joke with or tease someone
questions.explanation: 'To pull someone's leg' means to tease or joke with someone in a playful, harmless way. 'To physically drag' is wrong — the idiom is figurative. 'To trip someone' is wrong — it's not about causing physical harm. 'To help someone walk' is wrong — it means the opposite of assistance.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following idioms with their meanings:

Column I:
(a) To see eye to eye
(b) To be in hot water
(c) To wear one's heart on one's sleeve
(d) To have cold feet

Column II:
(i) To be nervous or afraid before an event
(ii) To agree completely with someone
(iii) To be in trouble
(iv) To show one's feelings openly

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'See eye to eye' = to agree completely — matches (ii). (b) 'In hot water' = to be in trouble/difficulty — matches (iii). (c) 'Wear heart on sleeve' = to display emotions openly — matches (iv). (d) 'Cold feet' = to become nervous/afraid before doing something — matches (i). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b). Option 3 swaps (b) and (c). Option 4 swaps (c) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'To leave no stone unturned' means to try every possible way.
(ii) 'To put the cart before the horse' means to do things in the wrong order.
(iii) 'To smell a rat' means to enjoy cooking.
(iv) 'To take the bull by the horns' means to face a problem boldly.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'leave no stone unturned' means to make every possible effort. (ii) is correct — 'put the cart before the horse' means to reverse the proper order. (iv) is correct — 'take the bull by the horns' means to face a difficult situation directly and bravely. (iii) is wrong — 'to smell a rat' means to suspect something wrong or dishonest, NOT to enjoy cooking.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct idiom: After losing the match, the captain said, 'Don't worry, every cloud has a __________ lining.'
questions.explanation: The idiom is 'every cloud has a silver lining' — meaning every bad situation has some positive aspect or hope. 'Golden' is wrong — the standard idiom uses 'silver'. 'Dark' is wrong — that contradicts the optimistic meaning. 'White' is wrong — not the traditional idiom.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The phrase 'to be on cloud nine' means:
options: To be flying in an airplane
questions.explanation: 'On cloud nine' means to be in a state of extreme happiness or euphoria. 'Confused' is wrong — the idiom expresses joy, not confusion. 'Flying in an airplane' is wrong — it's figurative, not literal. 'Very tired' is wrong — it expresses happiness, not fatigue.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 'To move heaven and earth' means to make every possible effort.
Reason (R): The expression uses hyperbole (exaggeration) to convey determination — implying one would even move the impossible to achieve a goal.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — 'move heaven and earth' means to do everything possible. Reason (R) is also correct — it uses hyperbole (moving impossible things) to express determination. (R) explains (A) by showing how the figure of speech creates the meaning. Option 2 is wrong because (R) directly explains (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is correct. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following idioms relate to 'being dishonest or deceptive'?

(i) To play a double game
(ii) A wolf in sheep's clothing
(iii) To have an axe to grind
(iv) Straight from the horse's mouth

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'Play a double game' = to act treacherously, pretending loyalty to both sides ✓ (deception). (ii) 'A wolf in sheep's clothing' = a person who appears harmless but is actually dangerous ✓ (deception). (iii) 'To have an axe to grind' is wrong — it means to have a selfish motive or personal agenda, not necessarily deception. (iv) 'Straight from the horse's mouth' is wrong — it means information from a reliable/direct source, the OPPOSITE of deception.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following idioms with their meanings:

Column I:
(a) To nip in the bud
(b) To keep one's fingers crossed
(c) To burn one's boats
(d) To shed crocodile tears

Column II:
(i) To show false sympathy
(ii) To destroy all means of retreat
(iii) To stop something at an early stage
(iv) To hope for the best

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'Nip in the bud' = to stop a problem when it's still small — matches (iii). (b) 'Keep fingers crossed' = to hope for a good outcome — matches (iv). (c) 'Burn one's boats' = to eliminate any possibility of going back — matches (ii). (d) 'Shed crocodile tears' = to pretend to cry/sympathize without real feeling — matches (i). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b). Option 3 swaps (b) and (c). Option 4 swaps (c) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The idiom 'a storm in a teacup' means:
options: A great fuss over a trivial matter
questions.correctAnswer: A great fuss over a trivial matter
questions.explanation: 'A storm in a teacup' means an unnecessary commotion or overreaction about something unimportant. 'Severe weather' is wrong — it's figurative, not about actual storms. 'Strong tea' is wrong — 'teacup' is part of the metaphor for smallness. 'A violent argument' is wrong — while it involves a fuss, the key point is that the matter is TRIVIAL.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'To have a green thumb' means to be good at gardening.
(ii) 'To show the white flag' means to surrender.
(iii) 'To be green with envy' means to be very jealous.
(iv) 'To see red' means to be colour-blind.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'green thumb' means natural talent for growing plants. (ii) is correct — 'show the white flag' means to admit defeat/surrender. (iii) is correct — 'green with envy' means extremely jealous. (iv) is wrong — 'to see red' means to become very ANGRY, not to be colour-blind.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The phrase 'to cut corners' means:
options: To do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often reducing quality
To drive around a corner quickly
To reduce the size of a room
questions.correctAnswer: To do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often reducing quality
questions.explanation: 'To cut corners' means to save time or money by doing things less thoroughly, often compromising quality. 'Driving around a corner' is wrong — the idiom is figurative. 'Trimming paper' is wrong — not about physical cutting. 'Reducing room size' is wrong — not about architecture.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following idioms about 'time':

(i) 'Time flies' means time passes very quickly.
(ii) 'In the nick of time' means just in time, at the last moment.
(iii) 'To kill time' means to murder someone.
(iv) 'Better late than never' means it's better to do something late than not at all.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'time flies' expresses how quickly time seems to pass. (ii) is correct — 'in the nick of time' means barely in time. (iv) is correct — 'better late than never' encourages doing things even if delayed. (iii) is wrong — 'to kill time' means to spend time doing something unimportant while WAITING, not to commit murder.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: What does the idiom 'barking up the wrong tree' mean?
options: To pursue a mistaken course of action or direct accusations at the wrong person
To make loud noises in a forest
questions.correctAnswer: To pursue a mistaken course of action or direct accusations at the wrong person
questions.explanation: 'Barking up the wrong tree' means to be misguided in one's efforts or to blame the wrong person (from hunting dogs barking at a tree the quarry has already left). 'Training a dog' is wrong — the idiom isn't about dog training. 'Climbing a tree' is wrong — it's figurative. 'Making noises' is wrong — it's about misdirected effort, not noise.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 'Actions speak louder than words' means what people do is more important than what they say.
Reason (R): A person's true intentions and character are revealed through their deeds, not their promises.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — the proverb values deeds over words. Reason (R) is also correct — true character shows through actions, not mere talk. (R) explains (A) by providing the underlying philosophy. Option 2 is wrong because (R) directly explains (A). Option 3 is wrong because (R) is correct. Option 4 is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following idioms with their meanings:

Column I:
(a) To sit on the fence
(b) To have butterflies in one's stomach
(c) To bite off more than one can chew
(d) To hit below the belt

Column II:
(i) To feel nervous or anxious
(ii) To act unfairly
(iii) To remain neutral / not take sides
(iv) To take on more responsibility than one can handle

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: (a) 'Sit on the fence' = to avoid taking a side/remain neutral — matches (iii). (b) 'Butterflies in stomach' = to feel nervous — matches (i). (c) 'Bite off more than one can chew' = to take on too much — matches (iv). (d) 'Hit below the belt' = to act unfairly or make an unfair attack — matches (ii). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b). Option 3 swaps (b) and (c). Option 4 swaps (c) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: The idiom 'to give someone the cold shoulder' means:
options: To deliberately ignore or be unfriendly to someone
To pat someone on the back
questions.correctAnswer: To deliberately ignore or be unfriendly to someone
questions.explanation: 'Give the cold shoulder' means to intentionally treat someone with coldness or disregard. 'Offer a jacket' is wrong — the idiom is figurative, not about clothing. 'Injure shoulder' is wrong — it's not about physical harm. 'Pat on back' is wrong — that would be the opposite (encouragement).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following idioms express 'working very hard'?

(i) To burn the midnight oil
(ii) To work one's fingers to the bone
(iii) To rest on one's laurels
(iv) To leave no stone unturned

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: (i) 'Burn the midnight oil' = to work late at night ✓. (ii) 'Work fingers to the bone' = to work extremely hard ✓. (iv) 'Leave no stone unturned' = to make every effort (implies hard work) ✓. (iii) 'Rest on one's laurels' is wrong — it means to be satisfied with past achievements and STOP working hard (the opposite).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'The ball is in your court' means it's your turn to act or make a decision.
(ii) 'To throw in the towel' means to give up or admit defeat.
(iii) 'To keep the ball rolling' means to maintain momentum.
(iv) 'To play ball' means to literally play a sport.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: (i) is correct — 'ball is in your court' means it's your responsibility/turn to respond. (ii) is correct — 'throw in the towel' (from boxing) means to accept defeat/give up. (iii) is correct — 'keep the ball rolling' means to maintain progress or activity. (iv) is wrong — 'to play ball' idiomatically means to cooperate or agree to something, NOT literally to play a sport.
